title: CORR Insights®: Preoperative Pain Sensitization Is Associated With Postoperative Pillar Pain After Open Carpal Tunnel Release
abstract: Where Are We Now? Roh and colleagues [9] conducted a novel prospective study aimed at understanding patient factors associated with postoperative pillar pain after carpal tunnel release. After controlling for relevant demographic and clinical variables, the authors found that higher preoperative scores on Pain Sensitivity Questionnaire minor (a measure of pain sensitization) and lower pressure pain threshold (through clinical assessment) were associated with higher postoperative pillar pain at 3 months; by 6 months, only an association between pain sensitivity and pillar pain remained, and the amount of variance explained decreased from 17% to 13%. The authors address several important questions for both surgeons and patients: Why do some patients who undergo a simple, elective, protocolized, straight forward surgical procedure like carpal tunnel release (or in fact any elective minor hand surgery) recover well while others do not? Why do some patients report higher pain intensity and magnitude of limitations such as disability for the same objective level of impairment? How can we reduce this variability and improve patient outcomes? From decades of research, we know that psychological factors explain a substantial amount of the variation in pain intensity and the magnitude of limitations or disability. Among these, depression emerged as a risk factor for poor outcomes after minor hand surgery [15], orthopaedic trauma [13], and for severe pain in the general population [10]. Catastrophic thinking (the tendency to think the worst, ruminate, and feel helpless when experiencing pain) and pain anxiety (cognitive, behavioral and physiological apprehension in responses to pain) are associated with increased magnitude of limitations and pain intensity in many orthopaedic conditions [14]. These unhelpful coping strategies also predict the development of persistent pain and disability at 5 months to 8 months postorthopedic trauma, even after controlling for injury severity [13]. A recent systematic review [12] concluded that psychosocial factors, including depression and unhelpful beliefs about pain are independent risk factors for the development of persistent pain after surgery. The study by Roh and colleagues adds to the body of research on patient-related factors that impact recovery by using the Pain Sensitivity Questionnaire as a proxy for potential hypersensivity to explain differential surgical outcomes after carpal tunnel release. Where Do We Need To Go? Pain research continues to be split between mechanistic/biomedical and biopsychosocial comprehensive approaches. The terms “hyperalgesia”, “pain sensitivity”, and “pain threshold”, are believed by some [3] to reflect stable, underlining biological predispositions. Others consider them a function of psychosocial processes like anxiety and depression, as research has shown an association between scores on the Pain Sensitivity Questionnaire and both depression and anxiety [4,8]; depression is also associated with lower experimental pain threshold/tolerance to interoceptive stimulation (ischemic pain) [11]. This dichotomy is unhelpful and divisive. These associations are bidirectional and reflect a complex mind/body interaction that gives opportunity for a comprehensive, multidimensional approach that can best improve patient recovery and well-being—a common goal of both patients and surgeons. The most efficient and effective way to help orthopaedic patients improve physical function and get back to their normal lives, is by assessing and addressing modifiable psychosocial factors at the first and during subsequent visits, and providing comprehensive biopsychosocial treatments that account for the complex interactions among biological, psychological, and social factors. Assessing modifiable psychosocial factors before an elective surgery like carpal tunnel release provides an opportunity to decrease the variability in pain and limitations/physical function following minor hand surgery by addressing the specific and modifiable patient factors that are responsible for this variability. Ideal models of care are integrated and house a multidisciplinary treatment team that provides comprehensive and coordinates biopsychosocial care such as surgeons, psychologists, or physical therapists. Such integrated models of care are becoming mainstay in primary care practices and bypass barriers to psychosocial care such as long wait-time, and stigma associated with mental health referrals [7]. Orthopaedic surgeons can improve their patients’ care by adopting a biopsychosocial approach to orthopaedic treatment and using integrated care models. Advances in technology can also help with the delivery of cost-effective comprehensive care. Many orthopaedic practices currently use decision aids [6] to help patients choose the best treatment that fits their preferences and life circumstances. These decision aids need to include assessments of psychosocial, demographic, and clinical risk factors, and provide both short-term and long-term predictions for all possible choices available to patients from immediate surgery to psychosocial treatment to address modifiable risk factors followed by surgery. In this way, we can empower patients to take ownership of their own recoveries, which is an important predictor of health and wellbeing. The trajectory of recovery should also be accounted for. Even if pain or disability may improve by the 1-year point, individual (work, relationships) and societal (costs due to additional medical care) resources may be lost in the interim, contributing to patient suffering. Numersous approaches to addressing psychosocial factors exist now, from web-based interventions without a therapist [5], to individual live video programs [16], coaching or more traditional cognitive behavioral approaches [1]. Patients can choose the best approach based on their life circumstances. How Do We Get There? Developing comprehensive evidence-based healthcare models for orthopaedic practices requires a partnership between surgeons and psychologists, an openness to moving beyond scripted job descriptions, and a change in the language we use when working with our patients. Psychologists will need to spend time learning about the specific orthopaedic conditions, to earn their patients’ trust, and to better distinguish cognitive errors from adaptive thoughts. Similarly, orthopaedic surgeons are required to learn effective communication strategies so that they can discuss psychosocial factors with their patients and guide them toward accessing care focused on improving recovery and health. Medical schools are already changing curricula to provide training on biopsychosocial models of health and illness across specialties, including psychiatry and orthopaedics, and these efforts should extend through residency and continuing education efforts. Surgeons who are already in practice can seek consultations from psychologists and learn both verbal communication skills using simple language, mirroring, ensuring that the patients understood the information presented, verbalizing concern, instilling hope, communicating willingness to help and nonverbal skills using eye contact, posture, tone of voice, and facial expressions, which are associated with patient satisfaction and health [2]. Both surgeons and psychologists need to be aware of the stigma associated with mental-health concerns. Older terms such as “catastrophic thinking” about pain and “pain anxiety” can be replaced with the opposite constructs of pain like “self-efficacy” and “resiliency”. We can use our culture’s fondness for sports and replace terms such as “therapy”, “psychiatric or psychological care” with more positive terms such as “skills training” or “coaching”, and discuss building resiliency through continued practice, like building a muscle. As practitioners on the front lines, treating patients across the continuum of health from acute injury, self-limiting problems, persistent illness, or aspects of normal human aging, orthopaedic surgeons have the unique opportunity to improve health and well-being in their patients. The orthopaedic injury that brings the patient in can become the catalyst for learning resiliency skills with benefits that extend to the entire patient’s life, and potentially to their families and to society.

Full narrative

Published in Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research in 2018, this CORR Insights commentary focused on the clinical implication of preoperative pain sensitization for pillar pain after open carpal tunnel release. Its central message, drawn from the underlying study it discussed, was that higher preoperative pain sensitivity and lower pressure pain thresholds were associated with greater postoperative pillar pain, highlighting the relevance of patient-level pain processing in surgical recovery.

The article has accumulated a modest but visible scholarly footprint. OpenAlex records 3 citations, and the downstream citing literature is concentrated in orthopaedic and musculoskeletal pain contexts, including a later evidence-based review of pillar pain after carpal tunnel release. That pattern suggests the commentary has been taken up primarily within the same clinical conversation it helped frame.

Reuse signals are also present: the record shows 4 downstream reuse events, including article-level reuse and a biomedical article mention indexed by Europe PMC. These signals indicate that the piece has been encountered and incorporated beyond simple citation counts, though the overall volume remains limited.

The publication history includes an expression of concern issued in 2020 because it cites retracted work. That editorial flag does not erase the article’s place in the literature, but it does mean readers and later users should interpret its claims with caution. The record also shows open access availability through a green/open instance, which may have supported discoverability and reuse.
